title: Chapter 3 | Born Ready to Learn
text: CHAPTER 3 Born Ready to Learn It begins before memory. Before speech. Before we know the names of things or even understand that things have names. Our DNA does not pass generations of learning down to us but rather passes to us a magical learning architecture capable of learning at an incredible pace, just as it does not pass memories of how the world looks but rather the eye itself . Groundbreaking research by Stanislas Dehaene, PhD, at the Collège de France, has revealed that newborn brains arrive not as blank slates, but as sophisticated prediction engines, prewired and ready to map the world with astonishing efficiency. He is perhaps best known for his work on numeracy, consciousness, and the neurobiological underpinnings of learning—especially in infants and children. His ability to combine rigorous experimental science with sweeping, interdisciplinary insight makes him one of the most influential voices in modern brain science. In his remarkable book How We Learn , Dehaene distills decades of research to reveal that the newborn brain is a learning engine prepared to absorb and adapt with astonishing speed. 19 Sound familiar? We didn’t exactly build AI so much as we gave it the ability to learn. And what comes next is often surprising. Much of what we explore in this chapter comes from Dehaene’s insights, reframing how we understand the handoff from DNA to learning architecture in the human brain—and how that architecture forms the cognitive roots of intelligence. While Dehaene’s work focuses on biological intelligence, the parallels to artificial intelligence are striking. What follows is my mapping of his foundational insights onto the architecture of modern AI. Human Learning Architecture Virtually at birth, the entire structure of the learning architecture is already in place and ready to begin building its own model of the world around it. A two-week-old infant is watching the world; not passively, but actively. Its eyes dart not at random but with intent. Stanislas Dehaene, using that same fMRI technology we discussed earlier, has shown that even at this early age, the brain is lit up with expectations. 20 Not expectations in the adult sense—no desires or plans—but prewired frameworks. Foundations built not from experience but from evolution. The baby’s mind distinguishes between motion that suggests life and motion that doesn’t. It can already begin to tell the difference between a person and a rock. A rock can move but only if impacted by another physical force, whereas a person (or an animal) can move on its own. If a rock moved toward it without an obvious external force, the infant would be surprised. A Prediction-Response Engine at Birth This idea is astonishing when you pause to consider it. The brain is not a recorder. It is a prediction engine, a guesser . It starts life already shaped by millennia of survival experiments, passed on by DNA as a hyperefficient prediction-response learning system. Dehaene illustrates this beautifully in discussing a study involving expectations. 21 In the simplest version, infants watched a series of colored balls—say, five red balls—dropped into a clear container and slowly appearing out of an opaque space at the bottom. 22 When a red ball then appeared from the container, nothing changed in their behavior. But when a ball of a different color emerged, their attention sharply increased. Their gaze lasted longer. They looked back and forth between the container and the ball. Something was off. The outcome did not match what they had predicted. In more refined versions of the experiment, the researchers introduced probabilistic variation. 23 For example, say four yellow balls and one blue ball were dropped in. When the yellow ball appeared from the container, it aligned with the majority and matched the infant’s statistical expectation. But when the single blue ball came out instead, the infants again showed surprise—longer gaze duration, increased attentiveness, and in some cases, neurological markers of novelty response. Even at this early stage, the infant brain was sensitive not just to simple patterns but to probability itself—a remarkably nuanced feat for such an early infant brain. In another study, Dehaene and colleagues used fMRI to track neural activity, revealing that the infants’ brains responded with heightened interest to the unexpected outcome. 24 Their expectations were disrupted, and their learning systems kicked in. This wasn’t just reaction. It was a prediction engine adjusting to new data. The brain was saying, “That wasn’t supposed to happen.” This capacity isn’t passed down as stored knowledge—it’s deeper than that. What DNA encodes isn’t the facts we need to know; it encodes the machinery we need to discover them. The structure of a learning architecture—the layered, energy-efficient system that learns through prediction and surprise—is itself an evolutionary gift. We are born not with answers but with an entirely intact system for how to learn them. Dehaene compares the infant brain to the complexity of the eye: constructed by DNA to function immediately. You don’t teach an eye to see. It was born seeing. You don’t teach a brain to look for meaning. It is born asking. Language offers another miracle. A child born in Madrid will learn Spanish. A child born in Montreal may learn both French and English. But the machinery to learn either—or any—language is already there. The word order. The sound structures. The rhythm. All absorbed with less energy than a dim light. Every moment, the infant brain is running tiny experiments. “If this happens, then that should follow.” When it doesn’t, the model adjusts. And all this is happening while the child is still preverbal, with little means to communicate; yet inside, an extraordinary engine of learning is already constructing a predictive model of the world—layer by layer, moment by moment. Most parents will remember the moment their infant, while eating in a highchair, dropped the spoon over the edge of the tray and was at first shocked and amazed when it fell to the floor. The infant then repeated this behavior to find its margin (the tray will stop it) and the prediction pattern was formed. If ever the infant dropped a spoon over the side and it floated up instead of dropping to the floor, the infant would start adjusting the prediction model right away, but until that happens, no additional energy is spent on this known pattern when the next spoon or food drops to the floor. That does not mean the infant understands gravity but rather that they have a developed sense of its impact on their world. The baby’s behaviors may appear simple, but the neural machinery is laying down the foundation for a lifetime of adaptation and discovery. And, as you will see, this is foundational to how AI came to be. It is not just learning. It is learning to learn —the very skill that gives rise to culture, language, tools, and civilization … to human intelligence. And eventually, to artificial intelligence. So, what role does emotion play in intelligence and how will that appear in AI? OceanofPDF.com
